entry.title: When Learning Breaks
entry.content:
This article is about how groups, organizations, and honestly myself drift toward optimizing the wrong thing — even when everyone involved is smart, well-intentioned, and genuinely trying.

This is not a blame piece. Not about bad incentives or bad people. It’s an attempt to formalize a pattern I keep running into: at work, in conversations with friends, and during those moments where you realize you’ve been “doing well” without being sure at what.

Something feels off.
Not because people are irrational — but because success itself quietly changes shape.

The obvious story (and why it’s incomplete)

Imagine a small autarkic village. Each season, Mark faces a simple choice.

He can extract
skip maintenance, overfarm a little, take the short-term win.

Or he can maintain the shared land
repair irrigation, rotate crops, do the slow, unglamorous work.

Individually, extraction makes sense.
Collectively, maintenance is the only way the village improves.

Economics 101 stops here and says: align incentives.
Add a tax, a subsidy, a rule.

In organizations, this becomes KPIs, bonuses, targets, dashboards.
In social life, it’s approval, reputation, status.
In politics, it’s votes, power, ideology.

But the problem was never that Mark is selfish.
Mark would genuinely prefer the village to thrive.

What’s missing is not motivation — it’s learnability.

The hidden assumption: causal transparency

Most optimization arguments assume this:

If I change my behavior, I can observe the effect.

Let’s give that assumption a name.

Causal transparency
The degree to which you can infer the causal effect of actions from feedback.

Learning by trial-and-error works when:

  • the effect is visible (something actually changes),
  • the feedback is timely (it arrives while the action still feels connected),
  • the outcome is attributable (you can tell what caused what).

Supermarkets mostly have this property.
Move a product, sales change.

Social media often does too.
Post something people like, engagement goes up.

In these environments, success is obvious because feedback is obvious.

But many environments don’t work like this:

  • hospitals,
  • large organizations,
  • research,
  • relationships.

Here, feedback is delayed, noisy, and confounded.
The causal signal exists — but it’s hard to isolate.

When feedback stops defining success

From a neuroscience perspective, learning relies on a tight loop:

act → observe → update.

When that loop weakens, the brain doesn’t stop optimizing.

It changes what counts as success.

When the true objective is hard to observe, you optimize a proxy — not because it’s better, but because it’s learnable.

Throw shoes in a dark room.
The real objective is nothing breaks.
But you can’t see that.

So you optimize a proxy: no loud noises.

That proxy is imperfect — but it responds.

This is proxy learning.

It’s not stupidity.
It’s what intelligence does when reality stops answering clearly.

Epistemic structure (the second axis)

Some systems are dark by nature. You take actions, but you can’t easily tell whether things improved or quietly degraded. Epistemic structure is what prevents success from collapsing into guesswork.

Epistemic structure
The ways a system builds understanding without having to learn by damaging itself.

Instead of learning by breaking things, the system learns by:

  • thinking,
  • simulating,
  • remembering,
  • sharing explanations.

If you have a mental blueprint of your room, we could easily rationalize where we should throw the shoe without breaking anything.

Epistemic structure lets systems define success before failure makes it obvious.

Common forms:

  • accumulated memory,
  • simulations,
  • protocols and checklists,
  • social cues and shared experience.

With strong epistemic structure, proxies stay aligned with what actually matters. Without it, success gets defined by whatever produces feedback.

The quadrant (for my consultants)

Two axes:

  • Causal transparency: can I learn from local feedback?
  • Epistemic structure: can the system learn without breaking anything?

Four regimes emerge.

High transparency, high epistemic structure

Aviation maintenance.
Making that one joke you know never fails.

You could experiment — but there’s no need.
Success is already well-defined and well-understood.

High transparency, low epistemic structure

The supermarket.
Figuring out what jokes land with friends.

Immediate feedback.
Fast, intuitive optimization.
Success emerges naturally from interaction.

Low transparency, high epistemic structure

Hospitals, nuclear plants, drug development.
Using a joke you learned from a great comedian because you can’t afford to discover what works by bombing.

Trial-and-error is too dangerous or too slow.
Success is defined externally, through models, aggregation, and memory.

Low transparency, low epistemic structure

String-pulling organizations.
Repeating the same joke in different rooms, unsure why it sometimes works.

KPIs detached from reality.
Confident decisions with weak explanations.
Optimization continues — but success drifts.

Why this feels so human

This pattern isn’t just organizational.

It shows up in:

  • relationships,
  • health decisions,
  • politics,
  • personal life choices.

Whenever feedback is delayed and causality is opaque, humans don’t stop optimizing.

They redefine success as whatever responds:

  • attention,
  • dopamine,
  • approval,
  • momentum.

Confidence grows because the system is internally consistent — not because it’s correct.
From the inside, those feel identical.

Collective misoptimization is what intelligence looks like when learning is structurally impaired.

And unless a system deliberately engineers transparency or epistemic structure, drift isn’t a failure mode.

It’s the default.
entry.summary: How success quietly redefines itself once feedback becomes opaque.

entry.title: Expertise Is Not Optional
entry.content:
Proof-read by mam, so you’ve got this!!!

This article is about learning as a prerequisite for doing, and how the cost of mistakes changes once the systems we interact with become powerful enough to actually hurt us back.

This is not the usual “experts vs. LLMs” debate, nor another AI bias rant (we’ve mostly lost that one already, folks). Think of this instead as my own attempt to formalize an intuition I keep tripping over, and honestly a reminder to myself of why expertise quietly stops being optional once leverage enters the picture.

Two ways to learn

As far as I can tell from my own experience, there are only two fundamental ways humans learn.

1. Learning by observing (indirect learning)

A child doesn’t need to insult someone to learn that it hurts. Watching how others react, tone changing, faces tightening, silence falling, is often enough to build a model.

This is learning by observing. No direct action is required, just attention. Watching the world, extracting patterns, forming internal models.

It’s how we learn to understand social norms, learn from books, and survive school. It’s also why explanations exist, and why we ask friends or parents for advice, which we then confidently ignore.

2. Learning by doing (direct learning)

Then there’s the other way: learning by doing.

  • You fall off the bike.
  • You burn the food.
  • You send the message you absolutely shouldn’t have sent.

This kind of learning is slow, frustrating, and expensive.

But it’s also deep. It’s how we build intuition and judgment. It’s why experience exists.

Both modes are essential, but they are not interchangeable.

Learning by observing is cheap.
Learning by doing is costly.

Let’s formalize this just enough to make that distinction precise. From here on, I want to formalize my intuition. It may look complex, but it really isn’t.

Formal setup

Let:

  • \(S\) be any system you’re interacting with
    (a car, a company, a relationship).
  • \(u \in U\) be an action you can take
    (steer left, fire an employee, bring up that argument).
  • \(E\) be your level of expertise with the system
    (capabilities, experience, intuition).
  • \(P\) be the power of the system
    (speed, impact, irreversibility, emotional leverage).
  • \(C(u; P, E)\) be the cost of taking action \(u\)
    (hitting an Amsterdammertje, losing trust, turning a minor disagreement into a multi day discussion).
  • \(K(u)\) be the knowledge gained from that action
    (how to drive, manage people, communicate).

The key point is that cost is not intrinsic to the action alone.
It depends on both the power of the system and your expertise.

Axiom 1: Learning can introduce costs

Learning by doing means accepting:

\[C(u; P, E) > 0 \quad \text{in exchange for} \quad K(u)\]

We pay for learning.

Learning by observing means:

\[C(u; P, E) \approx 0 \quad \text{while still gaining} \quad K(u)\]

We gain knowledge without paying for it.

Axiom 2: Learning by doing requires bounded cost

For learning by doing to be safe, we need:

\[\sup_{u \in U} C(u; P, E) < \infty\]

In words, the upper bound on cost must be finite and acceptable. We only live once (I hope), and we can’t afford catastrophic mistakes.

This is why:

  • pilots train in simulators,
  • companies run small experiments,
  • people sometimes think before they speak.

Axiom 3: System power scales the cost of mistakes

Recall that \(P\) denotes the power of a system.

Then:

\[\mathbb{E}[C(u; P, E)] \propto P\]

The cost of mistakes scales with power.

  • A mistake in a notebook costs minutes.
  • A mistake towards clients can cost days.
  • A mistake in cars can cost lives.

Axiom 4: Expertise reduces the cost of mistakes

Let \(E\) denote expertise.

Then:

\[\mathbb{E}[C(u; P, E)] \propto \frac{P}{E}\]

Expertise doesn’t eliminate mistakes. It shrinks their expected cost, on average action \(u\) under system power \(P\) and expertise \(E\) leads to lower costs.

  • It’s seeing further ahead on the road.
  • It’s managing resources inside a company.
  • It’s knowing when to drop an argument.

Proposition: Learning by doing becomes unsafe when power outpaces expertise

If \(P\) grows faster than \(E\), then:

\[\sup_{u \in U} C(u; P, E) \to \infty\]

The costs explodes. A child can absolutely learn to drive by doing. Given enough time and feedback, the learning signal is there.

But the system has:

  • high power,
  • low expertise.

The issue isn’t the ability to learn. The issue is cost of error overwhelming expertise.

Theorem: Safe learning requires either low power or high expertise

Let us call an action \(u\) safe under system power \(P\) and expertise \(E\) if its expected cost stays below some tolerance \(\epsilon > 0\):

\[\mathbb{E}[C(u; P, E)] \leq \epsilon\]

In words, safe learning means acting and learning from acting at a cost we are willing to pay.

This condition can only be satisfied in one of two ways:

\[(P \text{ is small}) \ \lor \ (E \text{ is large})\]

Meaning that either we are dealing with:

1. Low system power \(P\)

Mistakes are cheap, reversible, and contained.

  • Taking a car for a spin in an empty parking lot
  • Rearranging desks at the office
  • Saying the wrong thing among forgiving people

2. High expertise \(E\)

Mistakes are anticipated, mitigated, or avoided.

  • Driving lessons with an instructor
  • Mentorship at work
  • Knowing when to drop an argument

There is no third option.

When power is high and expertise is low, learning by doing stops being learning. It becomes gambling.

Why this matters now

Modern tools, especially AI, massively increase \(P\). Expertise \(E\) does not scale automatically.

The mistake isn’t learning by doing, or using powerful tools to save time.
The mistake is allowing \(P\) to grow faster than \(E\).

Or put differently:

Learning by doing is great, as long as the thing you’re steering can afford your ignorance.

Not because experimentation is bad, but because power and expertise must scale together.

Corollary: Observation precedes action in high-power systems

When system power \(P\) is large and expertise \(E\) is still low, learning by doing can’t be the default. The only viable option is to learn by observing first.

In practice, this means:

  1. read into the complex material,
  2. reason about consequences before touching the real system,
  3. simulate actions where failure is cheap,
  4. then act carefully.

Observation is not a lack of initiative. Wanting to build the startup, send the email, or push the money printing idea is understandable. It’s just a bad idea to do so without knowing what you’re doing.

Observation is how expertise is built without externalizing the cost of ignorance. Not as gatekeeping, but as the minimum respect owed to systems powerful enough to punish carelessness.
entry.summary: When power is high and expertise is low, learning by doing stops being learning. It becomes gambling.

entry.title: Oscillatory state-space models as neurons
entry.content:
The idea I keep circling back to:

If an oscillatory state-space model behaves like a neuron at the level of dynamics, then a network of them should pick up brain-like behavior more or less on its own.

Neurons spike, obviously, but that’s just what we get to observe. Internally, neurons seem to spend most of their time in an oscillatory regime: phase, frequency, synchronization, entrainment. If a state-space model lives in that same regime, then spiking starts to look less like the computation itself and more like an output format.

The question that keeps me awake at night:

What if the neuron itself is best thought of as an oscillator?
At this point I’m not even sure if, once you zoom out a bit, almost everything looks oscillatory at the right scale.

The neuron as a dynamical system

At this level of abstraction, a single oscillatory state-space model already overlaps uncomfortably well with how neurons are often described:

  • there’s an internal state evolving continuously in time,
  • it has a characteristic frequency (or multiple),
  • the response to inputs depends on phase,
  • units can synchronize with one another,

That’s basically describing cortical dynamics.

In this picture, spikes aren’t the state they’re an output. A nonlinear, learnable, thresholded, point-process observation of a smooth internal trajectory. The important thing isn’t the spike itself, but the oscillatory state underneath that makes a spike more or less likely at a given moment.

Why oscillatory SSMs feel like a reasonable abstraction

Linear oscillatory state-space models sit in a nice in-between place:

  • the dynamics are structured and stable (no exploding or vanishing as long as eigenvalues behave),
  • phase and frequency are purely degrees of freedom
  • Internally the model stays linear; all the nonlinearity is pushed to the readout, which keeps things simple.
  • long-range temporal structure comes from the dynamics themselves, not memory tricks,
  • inputs naturally shift phase and amplitude,
  • synchrony and desynchrony show up without being hard-coded.

Seen this way, stacking oscillatory SSM layers isn’t really about depth. It’s about coupling multiple oscillatory dynamical systems.

The part that actually matters

If each oscillatory SSM really does behave like a neuron in this limited, dynamical sense, then networks of them naturally support things we usually associate with brains:

  • phase-based coding,
  • transient synchrony,
  • oscillatory gating,
  • entrainment to inputs,
  • resonance-driven selectivity,
  • long-range coordination without explicit attention mechanisms.

All while staying trainable, stable, and scalable.

Or maybe this is one of those ideas that only feels convincing when it’s late, let’s thing about it for one more night ;)
entry.summary: Fascinated by the neurobiological readings on how the brain builds a model of the world.
